problems.form_value: S1 how_used: 'The participant then edited it in a custom interface: direct edits to any line, a dropdown of alternative AI-generated lines ..., or deleting the poem and starting from scratch.' S2 how_used: 'a complete poem that the participant edited with the Study 1 interface'. S2 arm: 'received a complete AI poem and edited it.'
problems.source_says: Editing was optional. The instructions told human-AI participants that they could leave the AI poem as it is. The paper reports no data on how many participants edited the poem or how much. The form states editing as a fact and leaves out the option to submit the poem unchanged, so some rated human-AI poems may be unedited AI output. Study 2 followed the Study 1 procedure, so the same applies to its editor arm. The assignment itself (an AI poem plus editing tools, against no AI) is unaffected. The S1 arm description ('could edit') is correct.
problems.quote: This part is entirely up to you. You can leave the poem as it is, make only a few minor adjustments, or delete the poem and start from scratch.
problems.locator: p. 3, Results, Study 1 (instructions to the human-AI condition); p. 5, Results, Study 2 ('The study followed the same procedure as Study 1')

problems.field: studies[S1].ai_tool.how_used and ai_tool.role (rationale for ideas_supplied); reconciliation.differences[0].resolved
problems.form_value: 'ideas_supplied is the closest, because the study hands the participant AI-generated content before writing and the participant never prompts the AI'
problems.source_says: The participant's own text does drive the AI in the editor interface. Each line has 'Edit line' and 'Update' buttons (Fig. 1). After a participant edits and updates a line, the system returns a new list of alternative lines based on the edited line. Edits to lines 1 or 2 also make the alternatives for lines 3 or 4 rhyme with the new text. So the arm combines an AI draft with AI line suggestions generated from the participant's edits. This is the same kind of step that the form codes as suggestions in the co-creator arm. The premise behind ideas_supplied is wrong, and the role choice (ideas_supplied, suggestions, or other) stays open, as open_questions already says. The codebook defines ideas_supplied as handing participants AI-generated ideas or examples. It does not make 'never prompts' the defining feature, as the reconciliation says. Criterion 1 is unaffected.
problems.quote: if they directly edit and update one of the lines that they wish to browse alternative lines for. In this way, the dropdown list of alternative lines updates in real-time based on the newly edited line.
problems.locator: p. 3, Results, Study 1 (interface features); p. 4, Fig. 1 ('Edit line' and 'Update' buttons on each line)

confirmed.statement: (a) S1 states random assignment: 'Participants were randomly allocated to one of two experimental condition groups.' The form's quote is verbatim. The arms are human (n = 48) and human-AI (n = 48), between subjects, with the individual as the unit.

(a) S2 states random assignment: 'Participants were randomly allocated to one of three experimental condition groups.' The form's quote is verbatim. The arms are human (n = 51), human-AI (n = 50), and co-creator human-AI (n = 51), between subjects.
confirmed.locator: p. 4 (allocation sentence and human arm) and p. 5 (other two arms), Results, Study 2

confirmed.statement: (a) Both studies: 'Condition assignments were random in both studies, with randomization administered via front-end programming.' The sentence is verbatim and sits on p. 9, where the form places it. The study ran through one URL link shared on the Prolific advertisement.
confirmed.locator: p. 9, Methods, first paragraph on the page; p. 2, Results, Study 1 (URL link)

confirmed.statement: (b) S1 assigned AI help for the participant's own poem. Human-AI participants first received a poem produced by the algorithm, with tools to edit any line, pick alternative lines from a dropdown, and get rhyme-consistent alternatives. The poets rated the poem each participant submitted.
confirmed.locator: p. 3, Results, Study 1; p. 4, Fig. 1; p. 4 (rating set of 48 + 48 + 50 poems)

confirmed.statement: The S1 AI condition is 50 poems that the system generated alone as a benchmark. No participant was assigned to it. Its contrasts differ only in whose output is rated, and the form keeps them out of the core (S1-O2, question none).
confirmed.locator: p. 2 ('A third experimental condition (AI condition) was added'); p. 4 ('benchmark value')

confirmed.statement: (b) S2: the human-AI arm used the same system and original interface as Study 1 (a finished poem plus editing features). The co-creator arm chose three topical words from 100 sets, wrote line 1, and alternated lines with the system, with 'select candidate verse' and free editing at any stage.
confirmed.locator: p. 5, Results, Study 2; p. 5, Fig. 2 caption

confirmed.statement: (c) The tool is the Van de Cruys (2020) neural poetry generation system: a recurrent neural encoder-decoder trained on 500 million words of CommonCrawl text (15 thousand word vocabulary), with 2048 candidate lines per line and rhyme and topic constraints. The paper calls it 'a generative AI system' and names GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 as examples of 'a more advanced generative AI system'. It is not a large language model or an image generator. The form says so and flags it for Review 1. It produces text from topic words and from the participant's lines, which fits codebook section 1 (systems that produce text from a prompt, including writing suggestions built on language models).
confirmed.locator: p. 3, Results, Study 1 (architecture); p. 2, last paragraph before Results; p. 8, Discussion, limitations; codebook section 1

confirmed.statement: (d) The control arm matches the form. In both studies the human condition 'completed a poetry task unassisted', so ai none and ai_vs_bau are right.
confirmed.locator: p. 2, Results, Study 1; p. 5, Results, Study 2

confirmed.statement: (d) The S2 co-creator against editor contrast compares two interfaces of the same system, another AI configuration, so ai_design is right. The co-creator arm is the configuration the paper predicts will do better, and the paper calls the editor role the usual default, so the treatment and control arms are assigned correctly.
confirmed.locator: p. 4, Results, Study 2 (prediction); p. 5 (same system, redesigned interface); p. 2, Introduction ('as is often the case by default')

confirmed.statement: (e) Neither study is within-person. Each participant was allocated to one condition, so order randomization does not apply.
confirmed.locator: p. 2, Results, Study 1; p. 4, Results, Study 2

confirmed.statement: S2 ai_tool.name_model ('same system, redesigned interface') follows the paper's specific sentence: 'participants collaborated with the same poetry generation system used in Study 1, however, the interface was redesigned'. The paper elsewhere says 'a redesigned version' and 'a new poetry generation system'.

Arm counts in the assignment fields fit the text. S1 n_randomized is null because the paper does not say whether the 6 attention-check failures came before or after allocation. S2 has 51 + 50 + 51 = 152 with no failures, so n_randomized equal to n_analyzed is supported.

summary: Both studies state that individual Prolific participants were randomly assigned, between subjects, to write a poem unassisted or with the Van de Cruys (2020) neural poetry generator (pp. 2, 4-5, and 9), so criterion 1 holds, with the caveat the form already flags: the paper calls the tool a generative AI system, but it is a recurrent encoder-decoder, not a large language model. Two ai_tool details are not supported: how_used says participants edited the AI poem, but the instructions let them leave it unchanged and the paper reports no editing data (p. 3), and the role rationale says the participant 'never prompts the AI', but each edited and updated line makes the system return new alternatives based on the participant's text (p. 3, Fig. 1).
